claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about PrPC structure and localization.

claims.claim: Misfolding of PrPC into PrPSc occurs by a self-perpetuating process of templated conformational conversion.
claims.source: Misfolding of PrPC into its pathogenic isoform, PrPSc, occurs by a self-perpetuating process of templated conformational conversion and causes transmissible and invariably fatal prion diseases (Prusiner, 1982).
claims.evidence: This is a fundamental concept in prion biology, supported by citation to Prusiner, 1982.

claims.claim: PrPC is a prerequisite of prion-associated neurotoxicity.
claims.source: In these diseases, PrPC not only represents the substrate for conversion but also a prerequisite of prion-associated neurotoxicity (Büeler et al., 1993; Brandner et al., 1996; Mallucci et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental work.

claims.claim: PrPSc is prone to aggregation.
claims.source: In contrast to PrPC, PrPSc is prone to aggregation and is characterized by a high β-sheet content and partial resistance to digestion with proteinase K (PK).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about PrPSc properties.

claims.claim: PrPSc is characterized by a high β-sheet content.
claims.source: In contrast to PrPC, PrPSc is prone to aggregation and is characterized by a high β-sheet content and partial resistance to digestion with proteinase K (PK).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about PrPSc structure.

claims.claim: PrPSc is partially resistant to digestion with proteinase K.
claims.source: In contrast to PrPC, PrPSc is prone to aggregation and is characterized by a high β-sheet content and partial resistance to digestion with proteinase K (PK).
claims.evidence: This is a standard biochemical property used to detect PrPSc.

claims.claim: PrPSc constitutes an essential component of infectious prion particles.
claims.source: Moreover, PrPSc constitutes an essential component of infectious prion particles or 'prions' (Prusiner, 1982; Silveira et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational prion research.

claims.claim: PrPC acts as a neuronal receptor for neurotoxic amyloid-β oligomers.
claims.source: Recently, a central role in more common proteinopathies, such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), has been attributed to PrPC where it was shown to act as a neuronal receptor for neurotoxic amyloid-β (Aβ) oligomers (Lauren et al., 2009; Dohler et al., 2014) and a variety of other disease-associated β-sheet rich protein assemblies including PrPSc (Resenberger et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: PrPC binds to a variety of disease-associated β-sheet rich protein assemblies including PrPSc.
claims.source: Recently, a central role in more common proteinopathies, such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), has been attributed to PrPC where it was shown to act as a neuronal receptor for neurotoxic amyloid-β (Aβ) oligomers (Lauren et al., 2009; Dohler et al., 2014) and a variety of other disease-associated β-sheet rich protein assemblies including PrPSc (Resenberger et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Resenberger et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Binding of pathogenic oligomers to the flexible N-terminus of PrPC initiates a cascade of events that mediates neurotoxicity.
claims.source: Despite some degree of controversy regarding this receptor function and its relevance in AD (Balducci et al., 2010; Benilova and De Strooper, 2010; Calella et al., 2010; Kessels et al., 2010), binding of pathogenic oligomers to the flexible N-terminus of PrPC is thought to initiate a cascade of events that mediates their neurotoxicity and results in synaptic degeneration and neuronal loss (Resenberger et al., 2011; Larson et al., 2012; Um et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and represents a proposed mechanism.

claims.claim: PrPC is subject to two conserved proteolytic cleavage events under physiological conditions, termed α-cleavage and shedding.
claims.source: PrPC is subject to two conserved proteolytic cleavage events under physiological conditions, termed α-cleavage and shedding (Borchelt et al., 1993; Harris et al., 1993; Chen et al., 1995; Mange et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claims.claim: α-cleavage occurs in the middle of the PrPC sequence and produces a soluble N1 and a membrane-attached C1 fragment.
claims.source: While α-cleavage, occurring in the middle of the PrPC sequence and producing a soluble N1 and a membrane-attached C1 fragment, confers neuroprotection with regard to prion diseases (Lewis et al., 2009; Westergard et al., 2011; Turnbaugh et al., 2012; Campbell et al., 2013) and Aβ-associated neurotoxicity (Guillot-Sestier et al., 2009; Resenberger et al., 2011; Beland et al., 2012; Guillot-Sestier et al., 2012; Fluharty et al., 2013), the role of an extreme C-terminal cleavage in close proximity to the plasma membrane, termed shedding, remains enigmatic.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about α-cleavage.

claims.claim: α-cleavage confers neuroprotection with regard to prion diseases.
claims.source: While α-cleavage, occurring in the middle of the PrPC sequence and producing a soluble N1 and a membrane-attached C1 fragment, confers neuroprotection with regard to prion diseases (Lewis et al., 2009; Westergard et al., 2011; Turnbaugh et al., 2012; Campbell et al., 2013) and Aβ-associated neurotoxicity (Guillot-Sestier et al., 2009; Resenberger et al., 2011; Beland et al., 2012; Guillot-Sestier et al., 2012; Fluharty et al., 2013), the role of an extreme C-terminal cleavage in close proximity to the plasma membrane, termed shedding, remains enigmatic.
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: α-cleavage confers neuroprotection with regard to Aβ-associated neurotoxicity.
claims.source: While α-cleavage, occurring in the middle of the PrPC sequence and producing a soluble N1 and a membrane-attached C1 fragment, confers neuroprotection with regard to prion diseases (Lewis et al., 2009; Westergard et al., 2011; Turnbaugh et al., 2012; Campbell et al., 2013) and Aβ-associated neurotoxicity (Guillot-Sestier et al., 2009; Resenberger et al., 2011; Beland et al., 2012; Guillot-Sestier et al., 2012; Fluharty et al., 2013), the role of an extreme C-terminal cleavage in close proximity to the plasma membrane, termed shedding, remains enigmatic.
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: Shedding could be protective by reducing the substrate for prion conversion and the receptor for neurotoxicity.
claims.source: On the one hand, by reducing the substrate for prion conversion and the receptor for neurotoxicity, this proteolytic release of almost full length PrPC from the plasma membrane could be protective with regard to prion diseases (Marella et al., 2002; Heiseke et al., 2008; Altmeppen et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Recombinant or transgenically expressed anchorless PrPC antagonizes PrPSc propagation.
claims.source: Moreover, recombinant or transgenically expressed anchorless PrPC mimicking shed PrPC has been shown to antagonize both PrPSc propagation and Aβ neurotoxicity, respectively, thus indicating a protective activity by blocking toxic conformers and preventing their access to the cell (Meier et al., 2003; Calella et al., 2010; Nieznanski et al., 2012; Fluharty et al., 2013; Yuan et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: Shedding could accelerate prion disease by increasing production and spread of anchorless prions within the CNS.
claims.source: On the other hand, shedding could accelerate an ongoing prion disease by increasing production and subsequent spread of anchorless prions within the CNS.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis presented by the authors.

claims.claim: PrPSc can be shed from the cellular surface in vitro.
claims.source: In fact, PrPSc can be shed from the cellular surface in vitro (Taylor et al., 2009) and anchorless PrPC can, in principle, be converted to PrPSc, resulting in an altered type of prion disease in transgenic mice (Chesebro et al., 2005, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Taylor et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Anchorless PrPC can be converted to PrPSc.
claims.source: In fact, PrPSc can be shed from the cellular surface in vitro (Taylor et al., 2009) and anchorless PrPC can, in principle, be converted to PrPSc, resulting in an altered type of prion disease in transgenic mice (Chesebro et al., 2005, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Chesebro et al., 2005, 2010.

claims.claim: High expression of anchorless PrPC leads to formation of prions and a late onset neurological disease.
claims.source: High expression of anchorless PrPC leads to formation of prions and a late onset neurological disease (Stöhr et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Stöhr et al., 2011.

claims.claim: ADAM10 is the relevant sheddase of PrPC in vivo.
claims.source: While the in vivo identity of the protease(s) responsible for the α-cleavage of PrPC remains a matter of controversy (Vincent et al., 2001; Tveit et al., 2005; Taylor et al., 2009; Oliveira-Martins et al., 2010; Altmeppen et al., 2011, 2012; Beland et al., 2012; Liang et al., 2012; Wik et al., 2012; Mays et al., 2014; McDonald et al., 2014), we recently showed that a disintegrin and metalloproteinase ADAM10 is the relevant sheddase of PrPC in vivo (Altmeppen et al., 2011), as previously suggested (Parkin et al., 2004; Taylor et al., 2009) and subsequently confirmed (Wik et al., 2012; Ostapchenko et al., 2013; McDonald et al., 2014) by in vitro experiments of others.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the authors' prior work and multiple citations.

claims.claim: Depletion of ADAM10 in neural precursors abolishes shedding and leads to posttranslational accumulation of PrPC in the early secretory pathway.
claims.source: Using conditional NestinADAM10 knockout mice (Jorissen et al., 2010), we recently showed that depletion of the protease in neural precursors abolishes shedding and leads to posttranslational accumulation of PrPC in the early secretory pathway indicative of a regulatory role of ADAM10 in PrPC membrane homeostasis (Altmeppen et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the authors' prior work cited as Altmeppen et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Membrane levels of PrPC were increased 1.56-fold in the absence of ADAM10 in neuronally differentiated NSCs.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 1A, surface biotinylation experiments on neuronally differentiated NSCs revealed that membrane levels of PrPC were increased 1.56-fold (±0.12; SEM) in the absence of ADAM10 (n = 9 independent samples) compared with wild-type controls (set to 1 ± 0.13; n = 9).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Genetic reintroduction of Adam10 into NSC cultures of NestinA10 KO mice was sufficient to reduce membrane levels of PrPC.
claims.source: Moreover, genetic reintroduction of Adam10 into NSC cultures of NestinA10 KO mice was sufficient to reduce membrane levels of PrPC (0.95 ± 0.11; n = 8) and thus to restore physiological wild-type conditions.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Nucleofection of NestinA10 KO cells with a vector lacking the Adam10 cDNA did not affect PrPC membrane levels.
claims.source: Nucleofection of NestinA10 KO cells with a vector lacking the Adam10 cDNA did not show any effect on PrPC membrane levels (1.55 ± 0.18; n = 5).
claims.evidence: This is a control experiment shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Increased total PrPC levels were found in ADAM10 knockout MEFs.
claims.source: As expected, we found increased total PrPC levels in ADAM10 knockout MEFs by (i) immunofluorescence analysis of permeabilized cells (Figure 1C, upper part) and (ii) Western blot assessment of MEF lysates (Figure 1D, left part).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claims.claim: Colocalization was observed between ADAM10 and PrPC at the plasma membrane in wild-type MEFs.
claims.source: In non-permeabilized wild-type MEFs, colocalization could be observed between the protease ADAM10 and its substrate PrPC at the plasma membrane (Figure 1C, bottom row).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Shedding is impaired in ADAM10 knockout MEFs compared with wild-type MEFs.
claims.source: Results obtained with concentrated media and with immunoprecipitation of shed PrPC from media showed that shedding is impaired in ADAM10 knockout MEFs compared with wild-type MEFs (Figure 1D, right part).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Shedding of PrPC was absent in NestinA10 KO neurons.
claims.source: Confirming our previous study (Altmeppen et al., 2011), shedding of PrPC was absent in NestinA10 KO neurons while tga20 neurons showed increased levels of shed PrPC compared with wild-type controls.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1E and confirmed by prior work.

claims.claim: tga20 neurons showed increased levels of shed PrPC compared with wild-type controls.
claims.source: Confirming our previous study (Altmeppen et al., 2011), shedding of PrPC was absent in NestinA10 KO neurons while tga20 neurons showed increased levels of shed PrPC compared with wild-type controls.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Reduction of ADAM10 expression was accompanied by increased PrPC amounts in cortical homogenates at postnatal day 19.
claims.source: First, we analyzed PrPC levels in A10 cKO and littermate controls at postnatal day (P) 19. Reduction of ADAM10 expression was accompanied by increased PrPC amounts as revealed by Western blot analysis of cortical homogenates (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Differences in ADAM10 expression and PrPC levels between A10 cKO and littermate controls were not seen in the cerebellum.
claims.source: In contrast to the cortex, differences in ADAM10 expression and PrPC levels between A10 cKO and littermate controls were not seen in the cerebellum, a brain region not affected by our knockout strategy (Casanova et al., 2001; Prox et al., 2013) (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A and citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Increased PrPC levels in A10 cKO mice did not result from transcriptional upregulation.
claims.source: Increased PrPC levels in A10 cKO mice did not result from transcriptional upregulation as there were no significant differences in PrPC mRNA levels in the forebrain at P19 as assessed by quantitative RT-PCR (mean ± SD: controls: 5.96 ± 0.86; A10 cKO: 6.32 ± 1.04; p = 0.23; n = 5) (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Adult A10 cKO mice did not show differences regarding weight and body size compared to controls.
claims.source: In contrast to newborn A10 cKO mice (Prox et al., 2013), adult A10 cKO mice did not show differences regarding weight and body size (Figure 2D and Video 1).
claims.evidence: This is an observational finding supported by Figure 2D and Video 1.

claims.claim: Adult A10 cKO mice showed increased levels of PrPC in the cortex and hippocampus compared with their littermate controls at 35 weeks of age.
claims.source: Again, as shown at P19, adult A10 cKO mice also showed increased levels of PrPC in the cortex and hippocampus compared with their littermate controls, as assessed by immunohistochemistry at 35 weeks of age (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: A10 cKO mice are viable and show a temporally unrestricted posttranslational increase of PrPC in neurons.
claims.source: Taking these observations together, A10 cKO mice are viable and show a temporally unrestricted posttranslational increase of PrPC in neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings presented in Figure 2.

claims.claim: A10 cKO mice developed prion disease more than 40 days earlier than controls.
claims.source: Our intracerebrally inoculated A10 cKO mice developed prion disease >40 days earlier than controls, corresponding to a shortening of incubation times of ∼30%.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by survival data shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claims.claim: Incubation times until onset of terminal prion disease were significantly reduced in A10 cKO mice (103 ± 7 dpi) compared with littermate controls (146 ± 2 dpi).
claims.source: Interestingly, we found significantly reduced incubation times until onset of terminal prion disease in the A10 cKO mice (103 ± 7 days post inoculation (dpi); SD) compared with littermate controls (146 ± 2 dpi) (Figure 4 and Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by survival data shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claims.claim: Disease duration was comparable between A10 cKO mice (35 ± 4 days) and controls (40 ± 2.4 days).
claims.source: Clinical manifestations (starting with a neglect of nest formation and fur cleaning, followed by presentation of a stiff tail and gait abnormalities, and terminating with kyphosis, weight loss, and hypoactivity) and disease duration (35 ± 4 days for A10 cKO mice and 40 ± 2.4 days for controls) were comparable between A10 cKO and littermate control mice (Figure 4, Table 1, Video 1).

claims.claim: tga20 mice showed fastest disease development and had to be sacrificed between 59 and 65 dpi.
claims.source: In line with other studies (Fischer et al., 1996; Sandberg et al., 2011), tga20 mice showed fastest disease development and had to be sacrificed between 59 and 65 dpi (Figure 3) whereas mock-infected A10 cKO and control mice were taken out of the experiment at 200 dpi without any signs of prion disease (Figure 4 and Table 1).

claims.claim: Mock-infected A10 cKO and control mice were taken out of the experiment at 200 dpi without any signs of prion disease.
claims.source: In line with other studies (Fischer et al., 1996; Sandberg et al., 2011), tga20 mice showed fastest disease development and had to be sacrificed between 59 and 65 dpi (Figure 3) whereas mock-infected A10 cKO and control mice were taken out of the experiment at 200 dpi without any signs of prion disease (Figure 4 and Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claims.claim: Comparable levels of PrPSc were found in frontal brain homogenates of terminally diseased A10 cKO and control mice.
claims.source: In terminally diseased mice, comparable levels of PrPSc were found in frontal brain homogenates of both genotypes as assessed by Western blot analysis after digestion of samples with PK (Figure 5A).

claims.claim: No differences in the PrPSc glycopattern between terminally diseased A10 cKO and control mice were detected.

claims.claim: No differences in sizes of PrPSc core fragments between terminally diseased A10 cKO and control mice were detected.

claims.claim: Prion infection caused spongiform lesions, massive astrocytosis, and microgliosis in both A10 cKO and control genotypes.

claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by histological data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Similar levels of PrPSc immunopositivity were found at terminal stage of prion disease in A10 cKO and control mice.
claims.source: Similar levels of PrPSc immunopositivity were found at this terminal stage of prion disease (Figure 5C), thus confirming our biochemical data (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Prion-diseased A10 cKO mice presented with an extraordinarily high abundance of tubulovesicular structures (TVS).

claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Relative levels of total PrP were highest in tga20 mice (5.0 ± 0.3), with increased levels in A10 cKO mice (2.8 ± 0.4) compared with controls (set to 1 ± 0.1).
claims.source: Relative levels of total PrP were highest in tga20 mice (5.0 ± 0.3; SEM), with increased levels in A10 cKO mice (2.8 ± 0.4) compared with controls (set to 1 ± 0.1) (A10 cKO vs control: **p = 0.0022; tga20 vs control: ***p = 0.0005; A10 cKO vs tga20: **p = 0.0015) (Figure 6A).

claims.claim: Relative levels of PrPSc were significantly elevated in A10 cKO mice (3.9 ± 0.8), with moderate levels in littermate controls (set to 1 ± 0.2) and reduced levels in tga20 mice (0.6 ± 0.3).
claims.source: Surprisingly, relative levels of PrPSc were significantly elevated in A10 cKO mice (3.9 ± 0.8), with moderate levels in littermate controls (set to 1 ± 0.2) and reduced levels in tga20 mice (0.6 ± 0.3) (A10 cKO vs control: *p = 0.049; A10 cKO vs tga20: *p = 0.032).

claims.claim: A10 cKO mice showed significantly increased PrPSc formation compared with littermate controls and tga20 mice.
claims.source: In summary, A10 cKO mice showed significantly increased PrPSc formation compared with littermate controls and tga20 mice, which cannot solely be explained by increased neuronal PrPC levels.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Neuropathological changes in the forebrain, including spongiosis, astrocytosis and microgliosis, were more prominent in A10 cKO mice at 95 dpi.
claims.source: Neuropathological changes in the forebrain, including spongiosis, astrocytosis and microgliosis, were more prominent in A10 cKO mice (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by histological data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: A10 cKO mice showed prominent PrPSc deposits in cortical and hippocampal regions at 95 dpi while controls and tga20 mice showed only moderate levels.

claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: No significant differences in the activation state of Fyn and Erk1/2 kinases were observed in forebrain homogenates between tga20, A10 cKO, and littermate control mice at 95 dpi.

claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Significant upregulation of calpain expression was found in A10 cKO mice (1.78 ± 0.24) compared with littermate controls (set to 1 ± 0.07) and tga20 mice (0.93 ± 0.14).
claims.source: Interestingly, we found significant upregulation of calpain expression in A10 cKO mice (1.78 ± 0.24; SEM) compared with littermate controls (set to 1 ± 0.07; *p = 0.034) and tga20 mice (0.93 ± 0.14; *p = 0.022) (Figure 6D), thus correlating with PrPSc levels (Figure 6A,B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Calpain upregulation seemed to be specific for prion disease as no differences were detected in non-prion infected A10 cKO mice compared with age-matched wild-type controls.
claims.source: This seemed to be specific for prion disease as no differences were detected in non-prion infected A10 cKO mice (mean: 0.90 ± 0.26 SEM; n = 4) when compared with age-matched wild-type controls (set to 1 ± 0.19; n = 5; p = 0.7) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Prion titers increased with progression of disease and reached a plateau phase towards the terminal stage of disease.
claims.source: Titers of infectious prions increased with progression of disease, showed only some inter-individual variation, and reached a plateau phase towards the terminal stage of disease.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of bioassay results shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Prion titers were independent of ADAM10 expression.
claims.source: However, they were independent of ADAM10 expression since we did not find differences between the two genotypes.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on bioassay data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: At early time points (35 dpi) prion titers were low (mean: A10 cKO: 3.9 ± 0.2 logLD50; control: 4.0 ± 0.2).

claims.claim: Intermediate prion titers were seen at 60 dpi (A10 cKO: 5.0 ± 0.5; control: 4.9 ± 0.8).
claims.source: At early time points (35 dpi) prion titers were low (mean: A10 cKO: 3.9 ± 0.2 logLD50; control: 4.0 ± 0.2), intermediate titers were seen at 60 dpi (A10 cKO: 5.0 ± 0.5; control: 4.9 ± 0.8), and highest titers were observed in terminally ill mice (A10 cKO: 5.8 ± 0.2; control: 6.0 ± 0.2) (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by bioassay data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Highest prion titers were observed in terminally ill mice (A10 cKO: 5.8 ± 0.2; control: 6.0 ± 0.2).
claims.source: At early time points (35 dpi) prion titers were low (mean: A10 cKO: 3.9 ± 0.2 logLD50; control: 4.0 ± 0.2), intermediate titers were seen at 60 dpi (A10 cKO: 5.0 ± 0.5; control: 4.9 ± 0.8), and highest titers were observed in terminally ill mice (A10 cKO: 5.8 ± 0.2; control: 6.0 ± 0.2) (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by bioassay data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Significantly increased PrPSc amounts in A10 cKO mice at 95 dpi did not result in elevated prion infectivity titers (A10 cKO: 5.74 ± 0.05; control: 5.66 ± 0.08; p = 0.2).
claims.source: Interestingly, significantly increased PrPSc amounts in A10 cKO mice at 95 dpi (Figure 6A,B) did not result in elevated prion infectivity titers (A10 cKO: 5.74 ± 0.05; control: 5.66 ± 0.08; p = 0.2).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by bioassay data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: An apparently reduced degree of spongiosis was found in the cerebellum and brain stem of A10 cKO mice compared with terminally diseased littermate controls.
claims.source: Whereas for striatum we observed neuropathological changes typically found in terminal prion disease irrespective of the ADAM10 status, we found an apparently reduced degree of spongiosis in the cerebellum and brain stem of A10 cKO mice compared with terminally diseased littermate controls (Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).

results.result: ADAM10 depletion leads to increased membrane levels of PrPC in multiple cellular models. Surface biotinylation experiments in neuronally differentiated NSCs showed 1.56-fold increased membrane PrPC in ADAM10 knockout cells, which was reversed by genetic reintroduction of ADAM10. Similar increases were observed in ADAM10 knockout MEFs, with colocalization of ADAM10 and PrPC at the plasma membrane in wild-type cells and impaired shedding in knockout cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C39 and C83 provide converging evidence from multiple cellular models (NSCs, MEFs, primary neurons) using complementary techniques (surface biotinylation, immunofluorescence, Western blot, immunoprecipitation). The rescue experiment (C33) and appropriate controls (C34) strengthen the conclusion that ADAM10 regulates PrPC membrane levels.

results.result: A10 cKO mice show posttranslational increase of PrPC levels in forebrain neurons. Western blot analysis at postnatal day 19 showed increased PrPC in cortex but not cerebellum of A10 cKO mice. This increase was not due to transcriptional upregulation (no difference in mRNA levels) and persisted in adult mice at 35 weeks of age.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42, C44-C45 demonstrate increased PrPC protein levels without corresponding mRNA changes, supporting posttranslational regulation. The regional specificity (cortex vs cerebellum) matches the Camk2a-Cre expression pattern, and persistence in adult mice indicates a stable phenotype. The qRT-PCR data (C42) rules out transcriptional mechanisms.

results.result: ADAM10 deficiency dramatically reduces incubation times in prion-infected mice. A10 cKO mice developed terminal prion disease at 103±7 dpi compared to 146±2 dpi in controls (>40 days earlier, ~30% reduction), while disease duration remained comparable (35±4 vs 40±2.4 days). Mock-infected mice showed no disease at 200 dpi.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C50 provide robust survival data with appropriate controls (mock-infected mice, tga20 positive controls). The dramatic reduction in incubation time with unchanged disease duration suggests ADAM10 affects disease initiation rather than progression. Statistical significance is reported (p=7.6×10⁻⁷) and sample sizes are adequate (n=7-8 per group).

results.result: At terminal disease, A10 cKO and control mice show comparable PrPSc levels and neuropathology. Western blot analysis revealed similar PrPSc amounts, glycopatterns, and core fragment sizes between genotypes. Histological analysis showed comparable spongiform lesions, astrocytosis, microgliosis, and PrPSc immunopositivity in both groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C55 demonstrate that despite different incubation times, terminal disease endpoints are similar between genotypes. The glycopattern analysis (C52) argues against generation of a modified prion strain. Multiple complementary methods (Western blot, immunohistochemistry, histology) support this conclusion.

results.result: At matched time points (95 dpi), A10 cKO mice show significantly increased PrPSc formation compared to controls and tga20 mice. A10 cKO mice had 3.9±0.8-fold elevated PrPSc levels (p=0.049 vs controls), despite tga20 mice having highest total PrP levels (5.0±0.3-fold). Immunohistochemistry confirmed prominent PrPSc deposits in A10 cKO forebrain with more severe neuropathological changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C61 demonstrate a paradoxical finding: A10 cKO mice show highest PrPSc despite intermediate total PrP levels, while tga20 mice show lowest PrPSc despite highest PrP. This is supported by both biochemical (Western blot) and histological data with appropriate statistical analysis. The finding cannot be explained solely by substrate availability.

results.result: No significant differences in activation of Fyn and Erk1/2 kinases were observed between genotypes at 95 dpi.
results.evaluation: Claim C62 reports negative findings for proposed neurotoxic signaling pathways. While the data are clearly presented, the single time point analysis may miss temporally or spatially restricted activation. The authors acknowledge this limitation in their discussion.

results.result: Calpain expression is significantly upregulated in prion-infected A10 cKO mice. At 95 dpi, A10 cKO mice showed 1.78±0.24-fold increased calpain levels compared to controls (p=0.034) and tga20 mice (p=0.022). This upregulation was specific to prion disease, as non-infected A10 cKO mice showed no difference from controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 demonstrate disease-specific calpain upregulation correlating with PrPSc levels. The inclusion of non-infected controls (C64) strengthens the conclusion that this is prion-specific rather than a general consequence of ADAM10 deficiency. However, the authors note they failed to detect clear evidence of calpain activation (cleavage products), which somewhat weakens the mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: Prion infectivity titers are independent of ADAM10 expression. Bioassays showed prion titers increased with disease progression (3.9-4.0 logLD50 at 35 dpi to 5.8-6.0 at terminal stage) but were identical between A10 cKO and control mice at all time points tested. Notably, elevated PrPSc at 95 dpi in A10 cKO mice did not result in increased infectivity titers.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C70 and C102 demonstrate dissociation between PrPSc levels and infectivity titers. The bioassay data are robust (n=4-6 tga20 reporter mice per sample) and cover multiple time points. This finding suggests ADAM10 affects PrPSc formation but not the composition of infectious prions, though the authors acknowledge the exact composition of 'prions' is not fully understood.

results.result: ADAM10 deficiency impairs spread of prion pathology to distant brain regions. At terminal disease, A10 cKO mice showed reduced spongiosis and virtually absent PrPSc, astrocytosis, and microgliosis in cerebellum and brainstem compared to controls. At matched time points (95 dpi), tga20 mice showed widespread pathology in cerebellum while both A10 cKO and controls showed minimal cerebellar involvement.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73, C107-C108 provide spatiotemporal analysis showing impaired spread from inoculation site (striatum) to distant regions (cerebellum, brainstem). The matched time point comparison (C73) controls for disease duration differences. The gradient of pathology correlating with shedding levels (tga20>control>A10 cKO) supports a causal relationship, though alternative explanations related to ADAM10's other substrates cannot be completely excluded.

results.result: Prion-diseased A10 cKO mice show extraordinarily high abundance of tubulovesicular structures (TVS).
results.evaluation: Claim C56 reports increased TVS in A10 cKO mice based on electron microscopy. While the observation is clearly documented, the functional significance of TVS in prion disease remains unclear. The authors note this finding may enable future purification and characterization of these structures.

results.result: The spatiotemporal data suggest a correlation between PrPC shedding and efficiency of prion spread within the brain, with tga20 mice showing highest efficiency and A10 cKO mice showing least efficient dissemination.
results.evaluation: Claim C74 integrates findings from multiple experiments to propose a correlation between shedding levels and pathology spread. While the correlation is supported by data from three genotypes with different shedding levels, the mechanistic basis remains uncertain. The authors appropriately acknowledge that non-PrP-dependent effects of ADAM10 deficiency could contribute.

results.result: ADAM10-mediated shedding has a dual role in prion disease pathophysiology. Lack of ADAM10 reduces incubation times and increases PrPSc formation, but impairs spread of prion pathology within the brain. The authors conclude that proteolytic processing represents a master switch in prion disease pathophysiology.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C80, C112 represent the main conclusions integrating all experimental findings. The dual role is well-supported by complementary data: shortened incubation times and increased PrPSc formation (local effects) versus impaired spread (systemic effects). However, the mechanistic details of how shedding affects each process remain incompletely understood, and the relative contributions of PrP-dependent versus PrP-independent ADAM10 functions are not fully resolved.

results.result: Background knowledge and literature context for prion biology, PrPC processing, ADAM10 function, and prior studies. These claims establish the scientific foundation, cite relevant prior work, and provide context for interpreting the current findings.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1-C4, C10-C31, C75-C77, C81-C82, C85-C114) represent established knowledge, literature citations, and contextual information. They are appropriately supported by citations to prior work and are consistent with current understanding of prion biology. Some claims represent hypotheses or speculation (e.g., C24, C26, C97-C98, C100, C104, C111, C114) which are appropriately qualified by the authors.

results.result: Adult A10 cKO mice are viable with normal body size and weight, and ADAM10-mediated shedding controls PrPC membrane homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Claims C43 and C84 describe the viability of the mouse model and propose a homeostatic model. C43 is supported by observational data, while C84 represents a model integrating findings from this and prior studies. The model is reasonable given the data but represents an interpretation rather than direct experimental evidence.
